common_name: Atkinsii Snowdrop (Tall Early Vigorous Historic Snowdrop)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Atkinsii is a tall, early-flowering historic hybrid with large, elongated flowers on long pedicels, taller and generally earlier to bloom than the common single snowdrop.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. Atkinsii, a Victorian-era hybrid selection dating to the 1860s and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is prized among snowdrop growers for its notably tall stems and long, elegant flower buds that open earlier in the season than the common single snowdrop, often appearing while snow still lingers on the ground. It bulks up quickly by offsets into substantial clumps and is widely regarded as one of the most vigorous and reliable of the historic named snowdrops for naturalizing under trees and along shaded paths. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for the most reliable transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Viridapice bears unusually large flowers with distinct green markings at the tips of the outer petal segments as well as the inner, a heavier and more visible green mark than the typical species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, ideally beneath deciduous trees where they receive good light before the canopy leafs out. Viridapice, a long-cultivated Dutch selection and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, is distinguished by its large, rounded flowers marked with a bold green blotch at the tip of each outer petal segment in addition to the usual green marking on the inner segments, a heavier and more conspicuous green patterning than the plain white species. Its comparatively large blooms and distinctive marking make it a favorite among snowdrop collectors, and it flowers slightly later than the earliest hybrids, extending the late-winter display. Divide and transplant clumps while still in leaf ('in the green'), immediately after flowering while the foliage is still active, for the most reliable transplant success. Never dig from the wild; purchase only nursery-propagated bulbs.

common_name: White Splendour Grecian Windflower (Large Pure-White Anemone Blanda)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; White Splendour bears unusually large, pure white daisy-like flowers, larger and cleaner in color than the typical blue-violet species.

directions: Soak the knobby tubers briefly in lukewarm water before planting to rehydrate them, then plant 2 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. White Splendour, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, bears notably large, daisy-like flowers in a clean, pure white with a tuft of pale yellow stamens, a striking departure from the blue-violet tones of the wild species and one of the most popular named forms of the Grecian windflower for brightening the early spring shade garden. It flowers in early to mid spring, closing at night and in overcast weather, and spreads gradually by tuberous rhizomes to form an increasing carpet beneath deciduous trees before going dormant by early summer. It pairs beautifully with early daffodils and other spring bulbs. Once established, it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Radar Grecian Windflower (Vivid Magenta-Pink White-Eyed Anemone Blanda)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Radar bears vivid magenta-pink flowers with a sharply contrasting white eye at the center, a much bolder color than the blue-violet species or the white 'White Splendour'.

directions: Soak the knobby tubers briefly in lukewarm water before planting to rehydrate them, then plant 2 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Radar bears vivid, saturated magenta-pink daisy-like flowers with a crisp white ring encircling the central boss of stamens, giving each bloom a distinct target-like eye that sets it apart from the softer blue-violet species and the pure white 'White Splendour', making it one of the most eye-catching named color forms of the Grecian windflower. It flowers in early to mid spring, closing at night and in overcast weather, and spreads gradually by tuberous rhizomes to form an increasing carpet beneath deciduous trees before going summer-dormant. It combines well with white or blue anemone blanda cultivars and early daffodils for a layered spring display. Once established, it requires essentially no care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Whitewell Purple Snow Crocus (Vigorous Reddish-Purple Early Species Crocus)

planting.note: Plant corms in fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Whitewell Purple bears deeper reddish-purple flowers than the typical pale lavender species and is an especially vigorous, free-seeding selection for naturalizing under deciduous trees and in lawns.

directions: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, ideal for naturalizing beneath deciduous trees or scattered through turf that is not mown until the foliage yellows. Whitewell Purple, one of the oldest and most widely planted named selections of the early species crocus, bears flowers in a richer, more saturated reddish-purple than the soft silvery-lavender of the typical wild form, opening flat in sunshine to reveal bright orange stigmas and closing again at night and in dull weather. It is exceptionally vigorous and free-seeding, naturalizing readily into large drifts within a few seasons under favorable conditions, making it a mainstay for early-spring lawn and woodland-edge plantings. It flowers in late winter to early spring, often among the very first crocuses to open, and provides an important early nectar source for emerging bees. Once established it needs no supplemental care beyond allowing the foliage to die back naturally to recharge the corms.

common_name: Gravetye Giant Summer Snowflake (Extra-Tall Large-Flowered Snowflake)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Gravetye Giant is a notably larger and more vigorous selection than the species, with taller stems, bigger flowers, and more blooms per stem.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; summer snowflake tolerates soil too damp for most bulbs and is well suited to pond margins, low-lying beds, and stream banks. Gravetye Giant, named for the English garden where it was selected, is the outstanding named form of the species, growing noticeably taller and sturdier than the typical species and bearing larger, more substantial pendant white bells, each tipped with a small green dot, with several flowers clustered per stem rather than the two or three typical of unimproved plants. It blooms in mid to late spring, later than most other white spring bulbs, extending the season, and naturalizes readily by offsets into large, long-lived clumps that rarely need division. Its extra height and bolder flowers make it a superior choice over the straight species for borders, waterside plantings, and cutting.

common_name: Blue Spike Grape Hyacinth (Double-Flowered Fluffy Blue Muscari)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Blue Spike bears fully double, sterile flowers packed onto each spike for an extra-fluffy, denser look than the single-flowered species, and does not self-seed.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 inches deep in fall in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Blue Spike is a fully double-flowered selection of the common grape hyacinth, its tightly packed florets each bearing extra petal segments that give the spike a denser, fluffier, more tufted appearance than the single bell-shaped flowers of the ordinary species, in the same rich cobalt-blue color. Because the flowers are double and largely sterile, it produces little to no seed, so clumps increase slowly and reliably by offset bulbs only rather than spreading by self-sown seedlings the way the species can. It blooms in mid spring alongside daffodils and tulips and combines especially well massed at the front of a border or naturalized in light shade under deciduous shrubs. Allow the strap-like foliage, which emerges the previous fall, to yellow and die back naturally after bloom before removing it.

common_name: White Snake's Head Fritillary (Pure White Nodding Bell Fritillaria)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall, handled carefully as they dry out quickly, in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Alba bears solid, unmarked pure white nodding bells, lacking the checkered purple pattern of the typical species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall as soon as available, since the small, fleshy bulbs dry out and lose viability quickly if stored; site in moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, ideally in a damp meadow, streamside, or border where soil does not dry out in spring. Alba is the white-flowered form of the snake's head fritillary, bearing solid, clear white nodding bells that lack the distinctive checkered purple-and-cream pattern of the typical species, providing a cleaner, more luminous look for a white or moon-toned planting. It blooms in mid spring on slender, wiry stems above narrow, grassy foliage, and naturalizes well in moisture-retentive soil, gradually forming colonies by both offsets and self-sown seed. It is especially effective massed with the checkered purple species form for contrast, or naturalized in damp, unmown grass. Allow foliage to die back naturally after flowering before cutting it down.
